newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian retail sales surge to 2-year high.
newsitem.headline: Australian retail sales surge to 2-year high.

text.p: Australia's bargain-hunting consumers went on a shopping spree in July, pushing the monthly retail sales index up to a two-year high and denting hopes of an interest rate cut this week, economists said on Tuesday.
But the economists still see room for another rate cut this year following a 50 basis point cut in late July to 7.0 percent.
The 2.4 percent rise in July retail trade reported on Tuesday was six times stronger than the market had been expecting, and more than double the highest forecast.
It was the largest monthly rise since May 1994.
The Bureau of Statistics said a strong rise in department store sales accounted for about half the rise, and said this strength may have been due to an increase in clearance sales.
"The heavy spending in department stores reinforces the belief that Australian consumers have become very price conscious since the recession," State Bank of NSW chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
While economists expected some correction to the July rise next month, the data led to some re-evaluation of the weakness seen in retail trade during recent months.
The strong rise also cast doubt on the growing market speculation that interest rates would be cut this week after Tuesday's Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board meeting.
"If the figure had been weak, it was argued, then the case for a rate cut this week would have been strengthened," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
"Since the figure was so robust, there has been a considerable reassessment," he said.
That reassessment saw bond and bill futures prices fall heavily after the data, as they had been most aggressive in factoring in a rate cut this week.
Ongoing talk of a rise in U.S. interest rates also helped to weaken the local market. Ten-year government bonds closed at a yield of 8.30 percent, up from Monday's close of 8.12 percent.

Despite the strength of the July figure, economists found some signs of weakness in the data, saying the fact shops had to resort to clearance sales to boost turnover suggested underlying demand remained weak.
"Perversely, the strong July turnover figure may actually highlight the weakness of retail trade," Nomura Research senior economist Andrew Pease said.
"Department stores are only increasing their turnover when offering large discounts at clearance sales," he said.
Because of this, the retail news did not rule out a fourth-quarter rate cut and was quite supportive of ongoing low inflation, economists said.
With consumers reluctant to pay full price for goods and instead waiting for sales, retailers were being pressured not to increase prices, thereby keeping a lid on inflation.
Westpac Banking Corp senior economist John Peters said that despite the rise in retail sales, trend data remained weak and was consistent with a further slowing in economic growth.

"Against this backdrop of waning economic activity, and easing inflationary and wages pressures, we see the RBA cutting cash rates by another 50 basis points to 6.50 percent in coming months," Peters said.
